title: Progressive overload
text: To keep building muscle and strength, gradually make your training harder over time: add weight (about 2.5 kg on big lifts, 1-2 kg on dumbbells), add reps within your rep range, or add a set. A simple method is 'double progression': pick a range such as 8-12 reps; when you hit 12 reps on all sets with good form, increase the weight and start again at 8.

title: How many sets and reps
text: For muscle growth (hypertrophy), aim for about 10-20 hard sets per muscle per week, split over 2 sessions, with 6-15 reps per set taken to 1-3 reps before failure. For strength, use 3-6 reps with heavier weights and longer rest. For muscular endurance, use 15-25+ reps. Beginners grow well with as little as 6-10 sets per muscle per week.

title: Rest time between sets
text: Rest 2-3 minutes between sets of heavy compound exercises (squat, bench press, deadlift, rows), 60-90 seconds for isolation exercises (curls, lateral raises), and about 30 seconds in circuits. Longer rest lets you lift more weight and usually gives better muscle growth than very short rest.

title: Training frequency and splits
text: Training each muscle about twice a week works best for most people. Good splits: 2-3 days per week = full body; 4 days = upper/lower; 5-6 days = push/pull/legs (push = chest, shoulders, triceps; pull = back, biceps; legs = quads, hamstrings, glutes, calves). Pick the split that fits your schedule; consistency matters more than the split.

title: Beginner full-body program (3 days per week)
text: Day A: goblet squat 3x10, dumbbell bench press 3x10, one-arm dumbbell row 3x10, plank 3x30 s. Day B: Romanian deadlift 3x10, seated dumbbell shoulder press 3x10, lat pulldown or inverted row 3x10, glute bridge 3x15. Alternate A and B on non-consecutive days (e.g. Monday, Wednesday, Friday). Add weight when all sets reach the top of the range.

title: Warm-up
text: Warm up for 5-10 minutes: light cardio to raise body temperature, dynamic mobility (arm circles, leg swings, hip openers), then 1-3 lighter warm-up sets of your first exercise. Static stretching before lifting is not necessary; keep it for after the session or a separate time.

title: Recovery and sleep
text: Muscles grow while you recover, not while you train. Sleep 7-9 hours per night, leave about 48 hours before training the same muscle hard again, and take at least 1-2 rest days per week. Muscle soreness (DOMS) 1-3 days after training is normal; sharp or joint pain is not, so stop and rest or see a professional.

title: Training with pain or injuries
text: Never train through sharp pain. If an exercise hurts a joint (shoulder, knee, lower back, wrist, elbow), choose a pain-free alternative for the same muscle, reduce the weight or range of motion, and see a doctor or physiotherapist if the pain lasts more than a few days. A chatbot cannot diagnose injuries.

title: Training at home with little equipment
text: You can build muscle at home with bodyweight and a pair of dumbbells: push-ups, pike push-ups, bench dips, inverted rows, Bulgarian split squats, single-leg Romanian deadlifts, glute bridges, planks. Make exercises harder by slowing the tempo (3 seconds down), pausing, doing one-sided versions, or adding reps.

title: Cardio and fat loss
text: Cardio helps heart health and burns extra calories, but fat loss mainly comes from a calorie deficit. Aim for 150 minutes per week of moderate cardio (brisk walking, cycling) or 75 minutes of intense cardio, plus 7,000-10,000 steps per day. Keep lifting weights during a diet to keep your muscle.

title: Calories: deficit, maintenance, surplus
text: To lose fat, eat about 15-25% below your maintenance calories (TDEE), aiming to lose 0.5-1% of body weight per week. To build muscle, eat about 5-10% above maintenance (0.25-0.5% weight gain per week). For recomposition, eat around maintenance with high protein. Maintenance is estimated with the Mifflin-St Jeor formula multiplied by an activity factor, then adjusted from your real weight trend.

title: How much protein
text: Eat about 1.6-2.2 g of protein per kg of body weight per day to build or keep muscle, spread over 3-5 meals of 20-40 g. Good sources: chicken, turkey, lean beef, fish, eggs, Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, lentils, chickpeas, tofu, whey protein.

title: Carbs and fats
text: Fats should be at least about 0.6-1 g per kg of body weight (about 20-35% of calories) for hormone health. The rest of your calories can come from carbohydrates, which fuel training: rice, oats, potatoes, fruit, bread, couscous, legumes. Prefer whole, fiber-rich carbs most of the time.

title: What to eat before and after training
text: 1-3 hours before training, eat a meal with carbs and protein (e.g. rice and chicken, oats with yogurt, a banana and Greek yogurt). After training, have a meal with 20-40 g of protein and some carbs within a few hours. The exact timing matters much less than your total daily calories and protein.

title: Hydration
text: Drink about 30-35 ml of water per kg of body weight per day, plus about 500-750 ml per hour of training, more in hot weather. Light yellow urine is a good sign of hydration. Sip water during rest periods, not during a set.

title: Supplements
text: Supplements are optional. Well-supported ones: creatine monohydrate (3-5 g per day, every day), whey protein (only to reach your protein target conveniently), caffeine before training, and vitamin D if you are deficient. Fat burners and testosterone boosters do not work as advertised. Anabolic steroids and SARMs are dangerous and are never recommended.

title: Weekly meal prep and freezer storage
text: Pick one prep day (e.g. Sunday). Cook 2-3 proteins (chicken, minced beef, lentils), 2 carbs (rice, potatoes, pasta) and roasted vegetables in bulk. Portion into containers. Keep 3 days in the fridge (max 3-4 days for cooked chicken and rice) and freeze the rest for up to 2-3 months. Thaw in the fridge overnight and reheat until steaming hot (75 °C inside). Cool cooked rice quickly and never reheat it more than once.

title: Halal eating for gym goals
text: A halal diet works perfectly for fitness goals: chicken, beef, lamb and turkey from halal sources, all fish and seafood (according to most schools), eggs, dairy, legumes and grains. Avoid pork, gelatin from non-halal sources, and alcohol in cooking. Check whey protein and supplements for halal certification.

title: Practical fat loss tips
text: Fill half your plate with vegetables, eat protein at every meal, limit sugary drinks and fried foods, watch oil portions (1 tbsp = 120 kcal), plan meals in advance and keep weighing yourself 3-7 times per week, looking at the weekly average rather than daily changes. Never go below about 1,200 kcal (women) or 1,500 kcal (men) per day without medical supervision.

title: Eating healthy on a student budget
text: Cheap high-protein foods: eggs, canned tuna or sardines, lentils, chickpeas, white beans, chicken thighs, milk, Greek yogurt, oats. Cheap carbs: rice, pasta, potatoes, oats, bread, bananas. Buy in bulk, cook in batches, and use frozen vegetables, which are as nutritious as fresh ones.
